name: Langerhans cell
markers: Langerin (CD207; some dermal dendritic cells in mice carry it too)
Birbeck granules (rod-shaped organelles seen by electron microscopy; langerin builds them)
summary: A dendritic-cell-like cell of the epidermis, spaced out among the keratinocytes, with long arms that reach toward the surface to sample what gets in. It carries langerin and rod-shaped Birbeck granules. After a danger signal it travels through lymph vessels to the nearest lymph node. Whether it mostly starts or restrains immune responses is debated.
functions: Stays in the epidermis for years, held among the keratinocytes by E-cadherin. In mice most Langerhans cells arise before birth from embryonic precursors and renew themselves in place; they need TGF-β1 and the cytokine IL-34, which keratinocytes make, to develop. After heavy inflammation (ultraviolet light, for example) blood monocytes refill the network. In people, recipient Langerhans cells were lost and replaced by donor cells within about 100 days of a bone marrow transplant, so blood-borne cells can refill the human network too.

Samples the surface: it extends dendrites between keratinocytes, through the tight junctions just under the dead outer layer, and takes up antigen at the tips (shown in mice). Langerin, a C-type lectin that binds mannose-type sugars, delivers what it catches into Birbeck granules.

Acts as a barrier to HIV-1 in isolated human Langerhans cells: langerin captures the virus, takes it into Birbeck granules and degrades it. When langerin is blocked, the cells become infected and pass the virus on.

Leaves the epidermis when danger signals arrive. TNF and IL-1β (made in damaged skin) make it mature and give up E-cadherin. It then needs the chemokine receptor CCR7 to enter the dermal lymph vessels, and it reaches the draining lymph node later than dermal dendritic cells (mouse evidence). In people, TNF injected into skin cut the number of epidermal Langerhans cells within two hours, and human skin explants release them through dermal lymph vessels.

Shows antigen on MHC class II to naive CD4 T cells in the lymph node. The helper type it favours depends on species and test: in mice, Langerhans cells were needed for Th17 cells against Candida skin infection; human Langerhans cells in culture preferentially induced CD4 T cells that make Th2 cytokines.

In healthy human skin (tested with the person's own skin cells), resting Langerhans cells selectively activate the skin's resident regulatory T cells and make them divide. When a pathogen is present, the same cells instead activate and expand effector memory T cells and limit the regulatory T cells' activation.

Debated: how much Langerhans cells prime killer T cells. Human Langerhans cells in culture were efficient at priming and cross-priming naive CD8 T cells. In mice with herpes simplex virus in the epidermis, Langerhans cells did not prime killer T cells; CD8α+ dendritic cells and, in a later study, langerin-positive CD103+ dermal dendritic cells did.

Debated: whether Langerhans cells mainly start or restrain responses. Mice that lacked them had stronger contact allergy reactions in one model and weaker reactions in another, and they were dispensable for making hapten-specific effector T cells in a third; the answer depends on the antigen, where it lands and which other cells are present.

Debated: whether it is a dendritic cell or a macrophage. It now looks closer to a tissue macrophage by origin (embryonic precursors, local self-renewal, dependence on IL-34 and its receptor CSF1R), yet it behaves like a dendritic cell by travelling to lymph nodes and presenting antigen to T cells.
abundance: A small fraction of the cells in the epidermis, spaced out in a network with each cell reaching toward its neighbours. Not found in healthy blood. Dermal dendritic cells, which also carry langerin in mice, are a separate group in the layer below.
